title: Earth's Layers
keyIdea: Earth is made of layers, like a peach or a boiled egg. The outside layer is the crust, the rock we live on. It is very thin: about 35 km under the land, which is thinner than the skin on an apple if Earth were apple-sized. Under it is the mantle, about 2,900 km of very hot rock that is mostly solid but creeps very slowly. At the centre is the core, made of metal. The outer core is liquid metal and the inner core is solid metal. The deeper you go, the hotter it gets: the centre is about 5,000 °C.
familyTip: Cut a hard-boiled egg in half, shell on. The shell is the crust, the white is the mantle and the yolk is the core. Ask: which part is thinnest? Then look at a peach or a plum: the skin, the flesh and the stone make the same three layers.

visual.caption: Which layer is it? Drag each card, or tap it and then a box.

items: Under the oceans and the land

lab.caption: Flagship lab: drill to Earth's centre, name the four layers, order them by thickness and by heat, sort solid and liquid layers, and check facts.

kid: Earth is made of layers, like a boiled egg. The outside layer is the crust. It is the rock we live on, under the land and under the sea.
Under the crust is the mantle. It is a very thick layer of hot rock. The rock is mostly solid, but it is so hot that it creeps very, very slowly.
At the centre is the core. It is made of metal, mostly iron. The outer core is liquid metal. The inner core is solid metal, because it is squeezed so hard.
The crust is the thinnest layer by far. If Earth were an apple, the crust would be as thin as its skin. The deeper you go, the hotter it gets. The centre is hottest of all.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. This supports the National Curriculum in England (Year 3 rocks; Year 4–6 geography on volcanoes and earthquakes) and NGSS 4-ESS2 and MS-ESS2-1 on Earth's materials. Rounded values from the USGS and BGS: Earth's radius is about 6,371 km, the crust is about 5–10 km thick under oceans and 30–70 km under continents, the mantle about 2,900 km, the outer core about 2,200 km and the inner core about 1,220 km in radius.

The lab has five tasks. Children drill from the surface to the centre and meet each layer, place the four names on a cut-away drawing (with the crust drawn thicker so it shows), order the layers from thinnest to thickest using true sizes, order them from coolest to hottest, sort them as solid or liquid, and check three children's statements.

Common mistakes. Many children picture the mantle as a sea of liquid lava; it is mostly solid rock that flows only over millions of years, and magma forms in a few places near the top. Others think the crust is the thickest layer, because diagrams draw it thick, or that the core is cold or hollow. Watch, too, for the slip that the hottest inner core must be liquid: pressure keeps it solid.

practice.prompt: Which layer do we live on?
practice.hint: Which layer is on the outside of Earth?
practice.explain: We live on the crust, the thin rocky outside layer of Earth.

practice.prompt: A drill goes down {a} km. Then it goes down {b} km more. How far down is it?
practice.hint: Add the two distances to find how far down the drill has gone.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} km. The crust under land is about 35 km thick, so the drill is still in the crust if the answer is less than 35.

practice.hint: Think of the bars in the lab. Which one was so small you could hardly see it?
practice.explain: The crust is the thinnest layer, about 35 km. The mantle is about 2,900 km thick.

practice.prompt: Ben draws the crust {c} mm thick. The mantle is about 80 times as thick as the crust. How thick should he draw the mantle, in mm?
practice.explain: {c} × 80 = {=80*c} mm. That is why real-size drawings make the crust look like a thin line.

practice.prompt: Mia says the mantle is a sea of runny lava. Is she right?
choices: No, it is mostly solid hot rock
practice.hint: In the lab, did the mantle go in the solid box or the liquid box?
practice.explain: The mantle is mostly solid rock. It is very hot and creeps very slowly, but it is not a sea of lava.

pool.prompt: Which layer is at the very centre of Earth?
pool.hint: The core has two parts. Which part is in the middle?
pool.explain: The inner core is at the very centre. Around it is the outer core, then the mantle, then the crust.

pool.hint: One part of the core flows. Is it the inner part or the outer part?
pool.explain: The outer core is liquid metal. The inner core is solid, because it is squeezed so hard.

pool.hint: What happens to the heat as you go deeper?
pool.explain: It gets hotter the deeper you go. The centre is about 5,000 °C.

pool.prompt: The mantle is about 2,900 km thick. A drill has gone {d} km into the mantle. How many km of mantle are left?
pool.hint: Take the distance drilled away from 2,900.
pool.explain: 2,900 − {d} = {=2900-d} km of mantle are left. The mantle is very thick.

pool.prompt: Name the layers from the outside in.
choices: Crust, mantle, outer core, inner core
Mantle, crust, outer core, inner core
Crust, outer core, mantle, inner core
pool.hint: Start with the layer we live on and end at the centre.
pool.explain: From the outside in: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.

pool.prompt: What is the core made of?
pool.hint: The crust and mantle are rock. The core is different.
pool.explain: The core is metal, mostly iron with some nickel. It is far too hot for ice or water.

pool.prompt: Why is the crust drawn thick in most pictures of Earth?
choices: Because it is the thickest layer
pool.hint: Look at the true thickness bars. Would the real crust show up?
pool.explain: The real crust is so thin it would be a thin line. Pictures draw it thicker so you can see it.

pool.prompt: Leo says the inner core is liquid because it is the hottest part. What did he forget?
choices: It is squeezed so hard it stays solid
pool.hint: Think about all the layers pressing down on the centre.
pool.explain: The inner core is the hottest part, but the weight of all the layers squeezes it so hard that it stays solid metal.

pool.prompt: The crust under a town is about 35 km thick. A deep mine goes {d} km down. How many km of crust are still below the mine?
pool.hint: Take the depth of the mine away from 35 km.
pool.explain: 35 − {d} = {=35-d} km of crust are still below. Even the deepest mines do not get through the crust.
